patient.chief_complaint: Sudden worst headache of life while watching TV, 2 hours ago, vomiting, neck pain
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Walker is a 61-year-old retired nurse with hypertension, hypothyroidism, and polycystic kidney disease who presents with a sudden catastrophic headache that began while she was watching television at home at rest. She describes it as the worst headache of her life, instantaneous onset, rated 10/10. She immediately vomited and called her son who brought her to the ED. She has known polycystic kidney disease and knows that this condition is associated with increased aneurysm risk. Her brother died from a ruptured cerebral aneurysm 3 years ago and a cousin has an unruptured aneurysm found incidentally. Despite this strong family history, she has never undergone cerebrovascular screening imaging. She takes nifedipine extended-release for hypertension — this is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker in the same class as nimodipine, creating a significant drug interaction that requires nifedipine to be held. She also has a documented contrast allergy (mild rash) from a prior abdominal CT for her PKD, requiring premedication prior to CTA. She has neck stiffness and photophobia. She is a former smoker and quit 20 years ago. The combination of PKD and family aneurysm history represents the highest-risk familial pattern for cerebral aneurysms.

output.summary: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is associated with an increased prevalence of intracranial aneurysms, estimated at 4–12% compared with 2–3% in the general population. The risk is further elevated in ADPKD patients with a first-degree relative who has had an intracranial aneurysm. Major society guidelines recommend intracranial aneurysm screening with MRA in ADPKD patients with a positive family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Repeat imaging at 5-year intervals is suggested for initially negative screening in high-risk ADPKD patients. Clinical correlation recommended.
